newsitem.title: FRANCE: Killing sparks revolt against Algeria rebels - paper.
newsitem.headline: Killing sparks revolt against Algeria rebels - paper.

text.p: An Algerian newspaper said on Thursday that the massacre of 31 people in an Algerian town has sparked a revolt against Moslem rebels by civilians who have armed themselves with guns and iron rods to repel more attacks.

"Medea town, since before yesterday (Tuesday), witnessed a kind of uprising against armed groups...This reaction has helped topple the wall of fear of the demons of terrorism," said Al Khabar, Algeria's main Arab-language daily.

Residents of Ktiten district, where 31 people were reported slaughtered last Friday by suspected Moslem guerrillas, took up arms to challenge the guerrillas and were followed by citizens in other parts of the town, the newspaper said.
"With the help of the security forces, the residents have formed self-defence groups," said Al Khabar.

Al Khabar said suspected members of the ruthless Armed Islamic Group (GIA) posted leaflets on walls in Medea in which they warned they would attack again on Wednesday night, coinciding with the most holy night in the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
The warning prompted more residents to rally to self-defence groups to keep watch for possible rebel attacks, it said.

"Those who are caught helping al Djazaraa, the police and the gendarmes, we will kill like those slain in Ktiten," shouted one suspected guerrilla through a loudspeaker from a mosque in the outskirts of Medea, said Al Khabar.

Al Djazaraa is an Islamist movement seeking to root political Islam in Algeria's secular culture. Al Djazaraa's top leader, Mohamed Said, was killed near Medea in 1995 after a failed attempt to unite forces with GIA.
The Algerian Jihad Islamic Front (FIDA), al Djazaraa's armed wing, last week claimed responsibility for killing Algeria's main union chief Abdelhak Benhamouda in central Algiers on January 28.
Hundreds of villages and remote small towns throughout Algeria have set up self-defence groups at the behest of the army commanders to fight Moslem guerrillas.
Most of these groups are led by fighters from Algeria's 1954 to 1962 war of independence against France.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
